introduction-trust-but-verify.core: IaC is code, so it can be tested, but infra tests trade speed for realism. The IaC test pyramid: fast static checks (fmt, validate, tflint, security scanners) on every commit; plan-level policy tests that inspect the planned changes; unit tests of modules (terraform test with mocks); and slower integration tests that deploy real resources, verify behaviour, then destroy them.

first_principles.problem: A module change passes review but deploys a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 in production.

analogy.title: Spell-check, editor, and test readers
analogy.story: Spell-check is instant, an editor catches logic, and test readers reveal how it lands in reality.
analogy.breaks: Readers are cheap; real cloud resources cost money.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Most bugs caught in the first minute.

check.q: Why not rely only on integration tests?
check.a: They're slow and costly; static and plan checks catch most issues in seconds and give faster feedback.

static-analysis-the-spellchecker-tflint.core: Static analysis inspects code without calling cloud APIs. terraform fmt and validate catch syntax and type errors; TFLint with provider rulesets catches invalid instance types, deprecated syntax and naming violations; security scanners (Checkov, Trivy, the successor to tfsec) flag risky settings such as public buckets or missing encryption. All run in seconds in pre-commit and CI.

first_principles.problem: A typo'd instance type 't3.mircro' passes validate and fails only at apply in CI.
truths: Many errors are visible in code.
derivation: **Fail CI** on findings with justified skips.

analogy.title: A spell- and grammar-checker
analogy.story: It underlines mistakes as you type, long before an editor reads the draft.
analogy.breaks: Spell-checkers miss meaning; static tools miss runtime behaviour.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Typo caught in seconds, before any plan.

code.text:
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform init -backend=false && terraform validate
tflint --init && tflint --recursive
checkov -d . --framework terraform --quiet
# Error: "t3.mircro" is an invalid value as instance_type (aws_instance_invalid_type)

check.q: What can TFLint catch that terraform validate can't?
check.a: Provider-specific invalid values (like non-existent instance types), deprecated patterns and custom naming rules.

plan-analysis-the-guardrail-opa.core: Static code analysis can't see computed values or module internals; the plan can. `terraform show -json plan.out` produces a machine-readable list of resource changes with before and after values. Policies in OPA/Rego (run by conftest), Sentinel or Checkov evaluate it to block dangerous changes, such as deleting databases, opening 0.0.0.0/0, or missing tags, before apply.

first_principles.problem: A variable default deep inside a module opens SSH to the world, and code scanners miss it.
truths: Some changes are only dangerous in context (deletes).

analogy.title: An airport X-ray of the packed bag
analogy.story: Checking the packing list misses what's actually inside; the scanner sees the final contents.
analogy.breaks: X-rays can miss things; policies only catch what they're written to check.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any plan replacing or deleting a DB fails CI.

code.text:
package main
import rego.v1

deny contains msg if {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
  "delete" in rc.change.actions
  msg := sprintf("%s would be deleted", [rc.address])
}
# terraform show -json tf.plan > plan.json && conftest test plan.json

check.q: Why analyse the plan rather than just the source code?
check.a: The plan contains resolved values and module internals, plus the actions (create/delete/replace), which source scanning can't see.

integration-testing-the-real-deal-terrat.core: Integration tests deploy real infrastructure in a sandbox account, check it behaves correctly (HTTP returns 200, the bucket rejects public access, a DB accepts connections), then destroy it. Terratest (Go) wraps terraform init/apply/destroy with helpers and retries, and the native `terraform test` command with run blocks can also apply real resources. Use unique names and always defer destroy.

first_principles.problem: A module produces a valid plan but the load balancer health checks fail because the security group blocks the target port.
truths: Tests must clean up after themselves.
derivation: Assert **behaviour**, with retries for eventual consistency.

analogy.title: A dress rehearsal
analogy.story: The script reads fine, but only a full run on stage shows the door doesn't open.
analogy.breaks: Rehearsals are cheap; cloud resources cost money, so clean up.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Proves the module actually serves traffic.

check.q: Why use retries in integration test assertions?
check.a: Cloud resources are eventually consistent; DNS, load balancers and instances take time to become ready.

structuring-tests-in-a-real-ci-pipeline.core: Arrange tests so the cheapest run most often. On every push: fmt, validate, tflint and security scans. On a PR: plan for each affected stack, plan-policy checks and module unit tests (terraform test with mock providers). On merge or nightly: Terratest integration tests in a sandbox, plus a leftover-resource sweeper. Gate production applies on all green.

first_principles.problem: Running full integration tests on every push makes PR feedback take 40 minutes, so engineers skip CI.
derivation: Run a **nuke job** for leaked resources.

analogy.title: Airport security lanes
analogy.story: Everyone passes the quick scanner; selected bags get a detailed search; full inspections happen offline.
analogy.breaks: Airports sample bags; CI should test every changed module eventually.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: PR feedback in ~3 min; full verification on merge.

code.text:
jobs:
  static:   { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ {run: make fmt validate lint scan} ] }
  plan:
    needs: static
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps: [ {run: make plan policy unit} ]
  integration:
    needs: plan
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps: [ {run: cd test && go test -timeout 60m ./...} ]

check.q: Where should Terratest-style integration tests usually run?
check.a: On merge to main or nightly in a sandbox account, not on every push, because they're slow and cost money.
